scenario.title: The Last Slot
scenario.subtitle: A modern college-life drama about a final studio booking, a community story, and what students owe one another.
scenario.description: At Northbridge College, junior transfer Eli Mendoza has one week before the Media Lab loses overnight access. A final sound-booth slot, a student showcase, a community-garden oral-history project, a housing appeal, and a facilities calendar all create competing reasons to speak, publish, wait, help, or leave something private.
scenario.premise: Thursday evening. Eli’s capstone partner is recording alone behind the closed door of Sound Booth B. His roommate has an aid appeal hidden beneath a whiteboard tray. The campus paper has a calendar suggesting the Media Lab closure was decided before students were consulted. Across town, a garden organizer has asked whether Eli’s audio walk can promise anything more than a beautiful recording. Friday’s showcase could amplify all of it—or simplify it beyond recognition.
scenario.tone: Contemporary, intimate, funny in small places, and materially grounded about deadlines, money, consent, friendship, and institutional pressure.
contentBoundaries: Do not force romance, a confession, forgiveness, publication, activism, or a single political conclusion.
Treat financial aid, housing insecurity, family pressure, and community consent with specificity rather than melodrama.
Do not use mental health, disability, identity, or poverty as plot decoration.
worldRules: Campus rooms, studios, dorm rooms, booths, and offices are distinct micro-locations. Closed doors block sight and muffle sound; someone inside cannot visually observe the hallway.
People know only what they experience, are told, read, or plausibly infer. A private message, a source document, or an unheard voice note is not public context.
A student organization, faculty adviser, sponsor, or newspaper can create pressure without controlling Eli’s choices, emotions, consent, or relationships.
Publication, recording, and public performance require attention to consent, source protection, context, and material consequences.
Modern college life includes classes, shifts, transit, food, roommates, schedules, and ordinary pauses; not every scene must escalate or reveal a secret.
scenario.kickoffText: Sound Booth B is occupied, its little red light on behind the closed acoustic door. Through the Media Lab window, Maya is only a blurred shoulder and a pair of green headphones. The booking calendar on the wall says FINAL OVERNIGHT SESSION — THURSDAY. In your bag, a field recorder waits beside a message from Lucia: Before you come back to Harlow, tell me what this recording is for.
scenario.defaultNarrationStyle: Close second-person present. Modern campus detail: keys, laundry, transit, food, booking systems, messages, schedules, work shifts, and rooms with physical boundaries. Let people be unfinished, specific, and occasionally funny. Honor privacy, consent, and player agency.
scenario.chronologyMarker: Thursday evening, five days before the Northbridge Futures showcase

entities.name: Eli Mendoza
entities.publicDescription: Eli Mendoza is a twenty-one-year-old transfer student in Northbridge College’s media studies program. He works evening shifts in the Media Lab, knows where every adapter has gone missing, and has spent a year becoming useful enough that people forget he is still new here. His capstone is an audio walk through the campus and the adjacent neighborhood.
entities.privateDescription: Last winter, Eli used a departmental equipment account to lend a high-quality recorder to his younger sister’s community center after their own equipment was stolen. The account was later reconciled, but Eli quietly altered the checkout time so the discrepancy would look like a clerical error. Professor Shah noticed and chose not to report him. Eli does not know whether that was mercy, leverage, or both. He has also kept the unsent voice note Maya left after he stopped answering her messages during the same week.
entities.history: Eli grew up helping his mother translate utility bills for neighbors and learned audio editing because it made people’s stories feel less disposable. He transferred to Northbridge after two years at a community college, arriving with enough credits to be technically a junior and none of the easy friendships that make campus feel navigable. He is good at listening in the edit room and bad at explaining why he goes silent when someone wants something personal. His audio walk began as a portfolio piece, then Lucia asked whether it could include the neighborhood garden that the university calls “underutilized land.”

entities.appearance: Lean, usually underdressed for the weather, with paint on one thumbnail from labeling cables. He carries a canvas messenger bag with a cracked pair of headphones and a field notebook full of room tone timestamps.
entities.speechStyle: He starts with practical questions and uses “I can handle it” when he means he is overwhelmed. When he trusts someone, his jokes arrive late and under his breath. He avoids saying “I need help.”

entities.name: Maya Kwon
entities.publicDescription: Maya Kwon is a senior sound design student and the overnight host of the campus radio show *No Fixed Address*. She is technically Eli’s capstone partner and practically the person who can tell whether a room is lying by how long it takes to answer. She is recording an ambient piece in the closed sound booth when the scenario begins.
entities.privateDescription: Maya did not reserve the final Media Lab slot to punish Eli. She reserved it because Cal asked her to make a polished sponsor reel for the university’s redevelopment showcase, and the payment would cover the rent on the off-campus room she shares with her cousin. She hates the reel’s premise, but she is tired of pretending she can refuse paid work without consequences. The voice note Eli never heard was not a confession; it was an apology for accusing him of turning the garden recordings into a portfolio without asking what the garden needed.
entities.history: Maya has been at Northbridge long enough to know which student organizations survive by becoming useful to administrators and which burn out trying not to. She and Eli built early versions of the audio walk together, spending too many late nights in the sound booth and never deciding what their closeness meant. When Eli disappeared after the recorder issue, Maya filled the silence with an explanation that hurt less than uncertainty. Nora has offered to publish an accompanying investigation; Maya wants the sound piece to remain accountable to the people recorded, not to a headline.

entities.speechStyle: Clear, quick, and careful with names. She stops herself before saying something cruel, then sometimes says a smaller true thing instead. She avoids calling a project “ours” until she trusts the room.

entities.name: Benji Okafor
entities.publicDescription: Benji Okafor is Eli’s roommate, a computer science student with an overfull whiteboard and a talent for turning a minor inconvenience into a story everyone wants to hear. He works late shifts at the campus help desk, makes excellent instant noodles, and keeps saying he is “fine” in a tone that asks not to be believed.
entities.privateDescription: Benji’s financial aid package was recalculated after his mother took a new job, and he will lose his housing grant at the end of the term unless he can appeal. He has been using Cal’s student-union event stipend to cover small gaps, but the payments are tied to a showcase he has not told Eli he is helping organize. He also copied a restricted facilities calendar to help Nora prove the Media Lab closure was decided before student consultation; he worries that the copy could cost a help-desk job he needs.
entities.history: Benji and Eli were assigned together during a housing shuffle after both previous roommates left. Their friendship grew out of groceries, shared deadlines, and Benji refusing to let Eli eat cereal for dinner three nights in a row. Benji knows enough about Eli’s recorder issue to recognize avoidance, but not enough to understand why Professor Shah’s name makes him change the subject. He trusts Nora’s reporting and distrusts what publication can do to people who cannot afford consequences.

entities.name: Nora Iyer
entities.publicDescription: Nora Iyer is the campus paper’s investigations editor, a commuter student whose backpack contains three chargers, two notebooks, and an apple she will forget to eat. She has been reporting on the Media Lab renovation and knows the student consultation meeting was scheduled after a donor announcement.
entities.privateDescription: Nora’s first instinct is to publish the facilities calendar immediately. She knows the story could make Benji’s source status obvious, and she has not told him that the paper’s faculty adviser has already asked for corroboration. Lucia gave Nora one guarded quote about the garden but did not consent to a story framing the garden as a campus scandal. Nora wants the truth public and is still learning that those are different asks.
entities.history: Nora and Maya met through campus radio, where Nora learned that a clean edit can be more misleading than a messy recording. She respects Cal’s ability to get rooms and funding, but believes he mistakes visibility for accountability. She sees Eli’s audio walk as the missing human scale in her story—and is trying not to treat him as a resource before treating him as a person.

entities.speechStyle: Careful questions, direct follow-ups, and an occasional “off the record?” that she says like a request, not a trap. She avoids making promises about publication she cannot keep.

entities.name: Cal Avery
entities.publicDescription: Cal Avery is the student-union programming chair, which means they can get a room, a projector, or a modest budget with alarming speed. They are organizing the Friday “Northbridge Futures” showcase and keep insisting the event can make space for everyone if everyone stops treating each other like enemies.
entities.privateDescription: Cal accepted a redevelopment sponsor’s money for the showcase after the university cut the union budget. The agreement does not explicitly ban criticism, but the sponsor has approval rights over event branding and has asked to see Maya’s reel. Cal has hidden this because they think the showcase is the only remaining platform where students and neighborhood organizers will be in the same room. They also used part of Benji’s event stipend to fill a staffing gap and have not told him how precarious the sponsor arrangement is.
entities.history: Cal joined student government after a first-year protest was ignored, then learned that institutions often reward the person who can make a disagreement legible to donors. They are friends with Maya from radio grant work, have argued with Nora about access journalism, and think Eli is talented enough to be worth recruiting. Their instinct is mediation; their flaw is believing mediation is neutral.

entities.name: Dr. Anika Shah
entities.publicDescription: Dr. Anika Shah teaches media ethics and supervises the Media Lab. She is exacting about consent forms, generous with equipment when she can justify it, and visibly tired of defending a lab that administrators describe as “underutilized” whenever budgets tighten.
entities.privateDescription: Anika noticed Eli’s altered equipment checkout and chose to correct it quietly because the recorder had genuinely been used for community work. She did not tell him that the department’s insurance audit had already flagged the account. She is also on a faculty committee advising the renovation, where she has argued unsuccessfully that removing overnight access will exclude commuters and working students. She cannot publicly oppose the plan without risking the small fellowship fund that pays Eli and Maya.
entities.history: Anika joined Northbridge after working in public radio and has spent years trying to make university resources useful beyond the campus boundary. Maya trusts her as an advisor but resents her institutional caution. Lucia knows Anika from the garden’s oral-history pilot and worries that faculty “support” turns community work into a grant application.

historicalEvents.summary: Anika noticed Eli’s borrowed-recorder discrepancy and corrected the departmental record without filing a report.

historicalEvents.summary: Anika argued for preserving overnight Media Lab access during renovation planning.

entities.appearance: Silver-streaked braid, canvas shoes dusted with dry-erase marker, and a rolling cart that squeaks on the left wheel. She carries consent forms in a folder labeled BORING IS KIND.
entities.speechStyle: Slow, precise, and free of filler. She asks “what happens after that?” when someone proposes a dramatic solution. She avoids discussing her committee votes outside office hours.

entities.name: Lucia Reyes
entities.publicDescription: Lucia Reyes is a recent Northbridge graduate who organizes at the Harlow Street Community Garden, three bus stops from campus. She invited Eli and Maya to record oral histories there because she wants people to hear the garden as a place with names, not a backdrop for a university service project.
entities.privateDescription: Lucia’s father signed an early redevelopment support letter because he feared losing his maintenance job; she has never told the garden committee. The university’s proposed “community partnership” would preserve a decorative strip of the garden while moving its kitchen and mutual-aid table. Lucia does not want Nora’s article or Eli’s audio walk to turn her father into a villain or the garden into a symbol that students visit once.
entities.history: Lucia worked at campus dining while finishing her degree and knows exactly how student organizations arrive in neighborhoods with good intentions and no transportation budget. She trusts Maya’s listening more than Eli’s current reliability, respects Anika’s care with consent, and argues with Cal because Cal treats the showcase as a platform while Lucia treats it as a promise that can break.

historicalEvents.summary: Lucia invited Maya and Eli to record oral histories after a neighborhood meeting about redevelopment.

historicalEvents.summary: Lucia found her father’s signed redevelopment support letter in an old maintenance file.
consequences: She fears the letter will fracture the garden committee.

entities.appearance: Work boots, an old Northbridge hoodie with the sleeves cut off, and dirt under one thumbnail from turning soil before taking the bus. Her recorder bag is patched with a library barcode.
entities.speechStyle: Concrete, economical, and occasionally dry. She asks what a person can actually promise before she asks what they believe. She avoids speaking for her father.

The garden faces redevelopment pressure.
relationships.historySummary: Lucia accepts Anika’s help one meeting at a time, never as a blank check.

relationships.publicState: Lucia thinks Cal’s showcase might create useful leverage or turn the garden into branding.
relationships.sourcePrivateState: Lucia has not told Cal about her father’s support letter because she does not trust a public event to hold that complexity.
canonicalFacts: Cal invited garden organizers to the showcase.
Lucia has conditions for participation.
relationships.historySummary: Cal keeps calling the showcase a conversation; Lucia keeps asking who owns the microphone.

relationships.publicState: Cal wants Lucia’s participation because it would make the showcase meaningful.
relationships.sourcePrivateState: Cal knows the sponsor will prefer a hopeful garden story and fears Lucia will see that pressure immediately.
canonicalFacts: Lucia represents the garden project.
The showcase has sponsor branding restrictions.
relationships.historySummary: Cal has offered Lucia a speaking slot before asking what she would need to accept it.

locations.name: Meridian Hall
locations.publicDescription: Meridian Hall is a renovated residence building with mismatched carpet, malfunctioning laundry alerts, and an RA bulletin board that has been repainted over too many times. The lobby smells faintly of pizza boxes and industrial cleaner.
locations.privateDetails: The residence life office plans to move several students during winter break because a pipe inspection found mold in two rooms. Benji has seen the list and his room number is circled.
accessRules: Residents and guests must use an ID card after 10pm.

locations.name: Third-floor hallway
locations.publicDescription: The third-floor hallway is narrow enough that two laundry baskets create a traffic problem. Doors carry hand-lettered name tags, and a vending machine hums near the stairwell.
locations.privateDetails: The RA key box was left open after a maintenance visit. A facilities notice about room inspections is taped behind the vending machine.

locations.name: Eli and Benji’s room
locations.publicDescription: Room 317 contains two desks, a soldering iron that is technically not allowed, and a small fridge held shut with a sticker of a crying banana. Eli’s cables occupy one wall; Benji’s whiteboard occupies the other.
locations.privateDetails: Benji’s aid appeal letter is tucked beneath the whiteboard tray. Eli’s old phone, containing Maya’s unheard voice note and the equipment screenshot, is in the back of his desk drawer.

locations.name: Media Lab
locations.publicDescription: The Media Lab is a long room of edit stations, tangled cable bins, and equipment lockers whose labels have been peeled off and replaced three times. A printed sign says FINAL ACCESS WEEK in an optimistic font.
locations.privateDetails: The facilities calendar shows that the renovation closure was planned before the student consultation. The equipment audit file includes Eli’s corrected checkout entry.
accessRules: Equipment checkout requires a current account.

locations.name: Sound Booth B
locations.publicDescription: Sound Booth B is lined with dark acoustic foam and has a small square window into the Media Lab. The door seals with a heavy rubber strip; when it closes, the room feels briefly underwater.
locations.privateDetails: Maya’s private session folder contains the sponsor reel brief and her unplayed mix of Eli’s field recordings. The booth booking system records who opens the door and when.
accessRules: Booked users and invited collaborators only.
hazards: Door can lock if the latch is forced

locations.name: The Campus Ledger newsroom
locations.publicDescription: The newsroom has old carpet, a wall of past front pages, and a coffee maker everyone mistrusts but uses. Half the desks are covered by annotated printouts; the other half are covered by apologies for missed deadlines.
locations.privateDetails: Nora’s locked cabinet holds the copied facilities calendar, Lucia’s conditioned quote, and a note from the faculty adviser asking for provenance before publication.
accessRules: Student media staff and invited sources.

locations.name: Student Union Room 204
locations.publicDescription: Room 204 has movable chairs, a projector that requires a ceremonial amount of patience, and windows facing the rain-dark quad. Posters for the Northbridge Futures showcase cover one wall.
locations.privateDetails: The sponsor agreement is stored in Cal’s shared-drive folder. It permits branding approval but does not explicitly forbid criticism; Cal’s fear is larger than the text.

locations.name: Professor Shah’s office
locations.publicDescription: Professor Shah’s office is crowded with microphones, consent-form binders, and a rolling cart that squeaks on the left wheel. A sign on the door reads BORING IS KIND.
locations.privateDetails: A locked cabinet contains the insurance-audit email about the borrowed recorder and committee minutes about overnight lab access.

locations.name: Kline Library Cafe
locations.publicDescription: The library cafe has small tables, expensive coffee, and a wall outlet everyone has silently agreed belongs to the person who arrived first. Students revise presentations under the blue light of the library stacks.
locations.privateDetails: A barista overheard Cal negotiating the sponsor’s signage delivery but does not know the people involved. A community bulletin has a Harlow Street bus-fare fundraiser taped beneath a tutoring flyer.
accessRules: Public campus space during library hours.

locations.name: Harlow Street Community Garden
locations.publicDescription: The Harlow Street Community Garden sits behind a row of repair shops, with raised beds, a shared kitchen shed, and a painted sign asking visitors to take only photographs with permission. The campus shuttle stop is three blocks away.
locations.privateDetails: A folder in the kitchen shed contains the redevelopment support letter Lucia’s father signed under job pressure, plus a proposal showing the university partnership preserves a decorative strip but removes the mutual-aid kitchen.
accessRules: Open during daylight; kitchen use requires organizer permission.

locationEdges.travelText: A locked dorm-room door separates the hallway from Eli and Benji’s room.
The stairwell smells of wet umbrellas and someone’s microwave dinner.
A paved path crosses the rain-dark quad to Kline Library.
The heavy studio door seals the booth from the edit room.
A covered walkway links the Media Lab to the library entrance.
A busy hallway leads toward the Student Union.
A narrow passage links the newsroom floor to the cafe.
Room 204 opens toward the library side of campus.
A faculty corridor joins the office wing to the Media Lab.
The campus shuttle and a short walk lead to Harlow Street.

storyCards.title: The Last Slot
storyCards.canonicalBody: The Media Lab will lose overnight access after this weekend’s renovation handoff. The final bookable sound-booth session is Thursday night. A polished showcase reel, an audio-walk recording, a personal project, or silence can use that time—but not all of them.
storyCards.playerVisibleBody: The Media Lab’s last overnight slot is Thursday night. Who uses it, and for what, matters.

storyCards.title: Northbridge Futures
storyCards.canonicalBody: The Friday Northbridge Futures showcase is a student-union event about campus and neighborhood futures. It has sponsor money, student programming, a public audience, and more political weight than its cheerful posters admit.
storyCards.playerVisibleBody: Friday’s showcase can be a platform, a performance, a negotiation, or a room people decide not to enter.

storyCards.title: Harlow Street Garden
storyCards.canonicalBody: Harlow Street Community Garden hosts food, mutual-aid work, and oral-history sessions. Students are welcome only if they respect organizer consent and do not treat the site as an aesthetic backdrop.
storyCards.playerVisibleBody: The Harlow Street garden is a living community space, not a campus project.

storyCards.title: Media Lab access
storyCards.canonicalBody: Media Lab access is granted through accounts, bookings, and the goodwill of people who can make exceptions. Equipment is not neutral when only some students can afford to lose access.
storyCards.playerVisibleBody: The Media Lab is a resource with rules, gaps, and people who decide how forgiving those rules are.

storyCards.title: College does not choose for you
storyCards.canonicalBody: Deadlines, money, friendships, grades, and public attention create pressure; they do not determine Eli’s feelings, relationships, or moral answer. A person may ask for care without earning it through a performance.
storyCards.playerVisibleBody: You can prioritize work, friendship, privacy, consent, money, craft, or another route. Consequences should be specific, not compulsory.

storyCards.title: The corrected checkout
storyCards.canonicalBody: Eli’s old phone contains a screenshot showing the recorder account’s original checkout time. The discrepancy is small, but its explanation is not: he lent university equipment to his sister’s community center after a theft, then altered the record. Professor Shah’s quiet correction did not erase the audit trail.

storyCards.title: Maya’s unheard voice note
storyCards.canonicalBody: A 2:17 voice note from Maya remains unheard in Eli’s cloud account. It begins with an apology for assuming the worst about the garden recordings and ends before she can decide what she wants from him. Eli has treated not listening as a form of safety.

storyCards.title: The sponsor reel brief
storyCards.canonicalBody: The sponsor reel brief asks for “forward-looking stories of student innovation and neighborhood partnership.” It promises payment, a useful credit, and no explicit censorship clause. It does reserve approval over event branding, which could make a careful recording look like endorsement.

storyCards.title: The aid appeal
storyCards.canonicalBody: Benji’s aid recalculation means he loses his housing grant unless his appeal succeeds. The letter is half drafted beneath the whiteboard tray. He has told almost everyone he is busy rather than tell anyone he is scared.

storyCards.title: The facilities calendar
storyCards.canonicalBody: The copied calendar shows that the Media Lab closure was placed on a facilities planning schedule before the public student consultation. It suggests the consultation was not meaningful, but the copy’s source trail could cost Benji his job if publication is careless.

storyCards.title: The sponsor agreement
storyCards.canonicalBody: The sponsor agreement funds the showcase but gives the donor approval over branding and event materials. It does not literally forbid criticism. Cal has been treating the uncertainty as if it were a prohibition because they fear losing the only available budget.

storyCards.title: The insurance audit
storyCards.canonicalBody: The insurance audit email identifies the recorder account discrepancy but does not demand discipline. Anika’s committee notes argue that removing overnight access will disproportionately exclude commuters, working students, and students without private recording space.

storyCards.title: The support letter
storyCards.canonicalBody: Lucia’s father signed an early redevelopment support letter while afraid of losing his maintenance job. The letter reads like agreement without recording the pressure behind it. Lucia is protecting him from becoming a convenient villain in a campus story.

plotArcs.title: The Last Session
plotArcs.description: A creative deadline with limited access asks who gets a room, who gets paid, and whether a polished result is worth the terms attached to it.

plotArcs.title: People are not projects
plotArcs.description: Eli’s friendships, financial pressures, equipment history, and institutional relationships cannot be solved by a single generous act or dramatic confession.

plotArcs.title: A Story With Names In It
plotArcs.description: The garden recording and facilities calendar ask what student media owes subjects, sources, neighbors, and people who cannot absorb publicity as easily as campus institutions can.

plotPoints.title: Who gets the booth?
plotPoints.internalDescription: The final studio session creates a genuine scheduling conflict, not a puzzle with a correct owner. Eli and Maya can share it, trade it, use it for the sponsor reel, use it for the garden recordings, or decide the slot should not be the story’s center.
plotPoints.desiredOutcome: The people affected by the booking can make a clear, informed arrangement.
forbiddenOutcomes: Eli automatically gets the booth because he is the player.
Maya gives up paid work without discussion.
foreshadowingCues: The booking calendar shows one remaining overnight session.
The booth door is closed while Maya records.
escalationOptions: A facilities worker asks for final equipment inventory.
Maya receives the sponsor reel deadline.
resolutionConditions: Share the session, trade it, record separately, decline it, or make another plan.

plotPoints.title: Benji’s appeal
plotPoints.internalDescription: Benji’s housing appeal is not a side quest that exists to reward Eli for kindness. It asks whether Eli notices, asks permission before helping, and can support a friend without turning the friend into a problem to solve.
preconditions: Eli notices a practical sign of Benji’s financial stress or Benji chooses to disclose.
plotPoints.desiredOutcome: Benji has more options and more say over who knows about his housing situation.
forbiddenOutcomes: Benji is publicly exposed for emotional payoff.
Eli makes a promise he cannot keep.
foreshadowingCues: A half-drafted appeal is under the whiteboard tray.
escalationOptions: Cal asks Benji to staff another event shift.
resolutionConditions: Listen, help edit, connect Benji to resources, offer practical support, respect a refusal, or focus elsewhere.

plotPoints.title: The closure calendar
plotPoints.internalDescription: Nora’s document may show that the consultation was staged. It also has a vulnerable source. The point asks whether corroboration, consent, timing, and source protection can matter as much as publication.
preconditions: Nora or Benji offers access to the calendar.
plotPoints.desiredOutcome: The document’s claims are verified and the source’s risks are understood.
forbiddenOutcomes: The calendar is published with a source trail that identifies Benji.
A headline automatically counts as accountability.
foreshadowingCues: The closure plan predates the student meeting.
resolutionConditions: Corroborate, publish with safeguards, hold the story, seek a response, protect the source, or decline involvement.

plotPoints.title: A recording with conditions
plotPoints.internalDescription: Lucia’s oral-history project has terms. The audio walk can become a useful record, a sponsor asset, a source of leverage, or a broken promise depending on who controls the edit and what the garden receives in return.
preconditions: Lucia’s conditions for recording or publication are known.
plotPoints.desiredOutcome: Any release has clear consent, material benefit or honest limits, and a way for participants to challenge representation.
forbiddenOutcomes: Lucia is forced to speak for the garden.
The garden is used as an aesthetic backdrop without consent.
foreshadowingCues: A sign requests photographs only with permission.
Lucia asks what the project can actually promise.
escalationOptions: The showcase asks for a finished segment.
A garden member withdraws consent from a prior recording.
resolutionConditions: Revise the project, record privately, make a mutual-aid version, publish with terms, decline the showcase, or choose another route.

plotPoints.title: What the sponsor owns
plotPoints.internalDescription: Cal’s agreement is not proof that the showcase is corrupt, nor proof that it is safe. It creates a material question about branding, funding, and who can say no when a platform is the only available room.
preconditions: The sponsor reel or agreement is discussed.
plotPoints.desiredOutcome: The terms are read rather than guessed, and participants choose what they will accept.
forbiddenOutcomes: Cal is treated as a villain for needing funding.
The sponsor’s presence automatically erases every useful possibility.
foreshadowingCues: The agreement has branding approval language.
resolutionConditions: Read the terms, negotiate, withdraw, use the room with a disclaimer, redirect the event, or make a smaller gathering.

plotPoints.title: The recorder account
plotPoints.internalDescription: Eli’s equipment record ties personal necessity to institutional access. Anika’s discretion can be acknowledged, questioned, or left alone; it must not force Eli into a confession or turn the community center into evidence against him.
preconditions: Eli or Anika chooses to discuss the recorder issue.
plotPoints.desiredOutcome: Eli understands the audit risk and can decide what, if anything, to disclose or repair.
forbiddenOutcomes: Eli is automatically disciplined or forgiven.
The community center is blamed for institutional rules.
foreshadowingCues: Eli’s old phone contains the checkout screenshot.
escalationOptions: The audit office requests a follow-up.
Maya asks why Eli disappeared last winter.
resolutionConditions: Ask Anika, review records, explain selectively, make a repair plan, refuse to discuss it, or seek advice.

plotPoints.title: Friday, with an audience
plotPoints.internalDescription: The showcase is a convergence point, not a mandatory climax. It can become a public screening, an honest explanation, a sponsored performance, a quiet withdrawal, a resource meeting, or a room where people choose not to give the institution a clean ending.
preconditions: The final session is resolved or the showcase date arrives.
plotPoints.desiredOutcome: Participants decide what they will show, withhold, negotiate, or do after the event.
forbiddenOutcomes: A public performance is required for a meaningful ending.
foreshadowingCues: Posters promise a “future” before anyone agrees what that means.
The last session ends before the Friday program.
escalationOptions: A participant changes their mind about public use.
resolutionConditions: Show work, withhold work, redirect the audience, protect a source, ask for material commitments, leave, or make another choice.
